newsitem.title: JORDAN: Iraq says U.N. inspectors spying, creating crisis.
newsitem.headline: Iraq says U.N. inspectors spying, creating crisis.

text.p: Iraqi Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz accused United Nations weapons inspectors on Thursday of trying to spy on Iraq's intelligence headquarters and fabricating a crisis over access to inspection sites.
Aziz, speaking in Jordan after talks with Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali, denied charges by chief weapons inspector Rolf Ekeus that Iraq had obstructed the inspections.

But he said Baghdad had stopped an American inspector from entering Iraq's intelligence headquarters, which he said was out of bounds to the inspectors because it dealt with the security of President Saddam Hussein.

"It's just a spying act," Aziz said. "We have not interfered but we cannot allow an American officer to enter into the political section of our intelligence headquarters under the cover of the special commission."
"Using American spies under the cover of the special commission is against the spirit and the letter of U.N. resolutions," Aziz added.

Ekeus steps down at the end of the month as head of the U.N. special commission (UNSCOM), set up after the 1990-91 Gulf War and charged with scrapping Baghdad's weapons of mass destruction and ensuring they are not replaced.
UNSCOM must certify Iraq has no weapons of mass destruction before the United Nations will lift trade sanctions imposed on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Ekeus said on Wednesday that Iraq was challenging the whole basis of the ceasefire agreement and called for a firm Security Council reaction to what he said was Iraq's repeated blocking of the U.N. weapons teams.
"In truth he came to manufacture a crisis in the last month of his tenure, to give the new head a situation of crisis so he takes a tough line on Iraq," Aziz said.
"He is lying. He is presenting facts falsely," Aziz said.
Ekeus said that when U.N. inspectors visited a university where professors were known to have been involved in a biological weapons programme, one of them tried to escape with a batch of papers.
The man was intercepted and the documents were found to relate to development of "a major biological warfare agent".
Aziz said the man in question was a young student who was running off with some examination papers to burn them.
He compared U.N. inaction over a major Turkish military incursion into northern Iraq with the international row over a few bits of paper.

"When Turkey violates (Iraqi sovereignty), America is silent. When a notebook is burnt... it's like the end of world at the Security Council... Britain and the United States (say) 'Iraq is violating U.N. resolutions'," he said.

Security Council sources in New York said U.S. envoy Bill Richardson was pressing for a tough resolution against Iraq but that such a move was likely to be opposed by Russia, China and Egypt, which have been more sympathetic to Iraq.
The Iraqi News Agency said Aziz had also accused Ekeus of deliberately delaying examinations of Iraq's missile engines parts in order to slow any lifting of U.N. trade sanctions.

"Such unobjective and costly delay is meant to postpone closing down of (Iraq's) weapons files to unidentified time...and prolong the embargo in order to continue the suffering of the Iraqi people," Aziz said in a letter to Ekeus.
